Ahmed is dead silent. He has been playing this game with the interrogators for days already. Irocco's response to the accusations of terrorism has only made these devils more intrusive and invasive. In a similar way, Hammad has refused to talk to the policemen beyond reinforcing the fact that he is a terrorist sponsored by Irocco, even if this may not be the case.[/quote]
Ahmed is annoyed, though this thought turns to terror as [b][i]he[/i][/b] walks in. The One who Inquires, they say, his department is just him, that he is immortal, that he will never die. Rumours swirl that he is Cain himself, atoning for his sins by breaking sinners. But all of that is less terrifying than the thought that he is a mere mortal.

The staff enters the room before him, and then the smell of fresh blood is intertwined with the old. His cloak, the bottom stained with crusted blood, flows into the room, the barbs around his neck bore the most stench, they still pierced his flesh. His great pointed helmet scrapes the ceiling. 

[b]"𝐘𝐨𝐮, so you're the so-called terrorist? Nothing but a scared boy."[/b]

He turns to the interrogators.

[b]"My 𝐌𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫, said that I am to ask permission before interrogating this mongrol, so, may I?"[/b]

A formality, a terrifying, condescending formality.

[b]The Resolution[/b]
Gentlemen, we are committing treason of the highest order by meetingthe manners and the likes of which have not been seen before, for though our treason to some may be heinous to others it is an act of God, The speaker was, James Mrjkanlwyth, the current standing president of the newly formed International Association for the Reunification of Rosenmarkke and Montfleur. The group had been formed in the disastrous aftermath of the Rosenmarkket-Wuloosyan war, which crippled Rosenmarkke and had left the delicately built regime in tatters. 

Gentlemen, what are our aims? asked another voice, rising from the bench of the dusty old Baptist church which they were meeting in, away from the prying eyes of the Rosenmarkket government, which, though disjointed, still held nominal powers to ensure the cohesion of the state was not further degraded. 

The aims? intoned yet another, this time a Montfleurois man, by the name of Mr. Z.

The aims are clear, intoned James, To free the people from the chains of the tyranny of the security state, to restore the ancient union between Rosenmarkke and Montfleur, and to build a stronger and more unified Eastern Elseyr! 

Yea! Yea! Yea! declared the group of men, rising and pumping their fists with raucous acclaim.

Gentlemen! Roared Joseph Madison, the most fervent of them, yet the least ideological, Let us be practical, let us be even headed, he continued, jeers filling the room.

It is necessary that the revolution is recognised internationally as one of freedom against a tyrannic government, not as a countercoup. I hear that one Will Rosec has, in a podcast of public hearing, declared that we seek to coup the government of Rosenmarkke in order to achieve our aims!

More jeers filled the room as canes and staffs were pounded, shaking the old oak boards and throwing dust from the ceiling.

Gentlemen, gentlemen, the honourable Madison has a point, replied James, We must secure political alliances, internationally and nationally, for right now our movement threatens to become disordered and malaligned, he continued as the men in the hall took their seats once more.

Now, the preliminary goal of this assembly is to ensure that the assembled and international press are made aware of our movement, whether in small text, or in ad, or in large font on the front pages of the news, continued the president, This will broaden our coverage and encourage support, 

The front pages? asked Mr. Z, who was wearing a powdered wig and waistcoat of white to match.

Yes, the papers and the international telecommunications network shall spread word far and near, we are not rats hiding in a hole, as the Mr. Rosec has suggested, we must come into the daylight, a murmur ran through the room. One Louis Meternisse rose from his bench with his hand lifted.

I support this motion, but I fear that there are enemies to Rosenmarkke, and perhaps to Montfleur, who might seize upon the disunity of our movement to turn it into a collapsing or annexing force,

A valid point, Mr. Meternisse, intoned Mr. Z.

But not a point of which we are concerned, the honourable Meternisse has no reason to fear repercussions from the enemies of Rosenmarkke, because we are achieving their very goals, replied Joseph Madison, to a few hear, hear.

I would wish to write a grievance of petition, said a gentle voice from the rear of the hall as the thin figure of one Mr. Lambeau stepped into the hall, his sharp nose and piercing blue eyes framed by a triple curl powdered wig.

A grievance of petition? In what manner? asked Mr. Z, his eyes narrowing.

And to whom? asked Mr. Meternisse.

To the government of Rosenmarkke, the Council of 99, replied Lambeau, Gentlemen, such a matter will be most indubitably unable to be ignored, if an organisation of our size and our internationality and of our composition wrote it,

I find these claims dubious, intoned the president, We are hardly fifty men, and perhaps a few subscribed to our newsletter, pray do tell what do you mean by the term internationality? 

I meant our composition, Mr. President, we are an international bunch, with connections, and many to many powers and placeseven though we are smallthe mouse still caused the plague, 

A few chuckles ran around the hall.

Mr. Lambeau, what exactly would you consider putting in the grievance of petition? asked Meternisse.

We would list all the crimes by which the government of Rosenmarkke has oppressed its people, it is sure to do rounds in the more liberally minded nations, stated Lambeau.

But evidence is paramount to any claim, retorted  Mr. Z.

Then we gather evidence, the regime is collapsing, there are civil servants who are leaving, there are former SCSID officers and informants who seek to restore order, the table is turned to our side, gentlemen, replied Lambeau.

Let me perceive your point, Mr. Lambeau, replied the president, You wish to engage with the state, to complain to the state about the state, 

An uneasy silence filled the hall as the logic of the idea was violently imposed upon the minds of those assembled.

If you put it that waythen yes, replied Lambeau with a frown, I do apologise, 

It is no matter, let us get to the topic of the hand, replied the president with a stern nod, The propagation of any good revolt is through the media, people see our claims, they see our organisaton, they perhaps are curious or perhaps seek to support us, and thus our numbers grow and the eyes of the world turn not towards that old order, but to the order that is now being formed, he continued.

Mr. President, if I may speak, said Mr. Z, rising from his seat.

This consortium is disorganised, it hasnt even brought forward the means or ways by which to consult with the governments involved, while the Rosenmarkket government perhaps is fracturedthe Montfleurois government is most certainly united and stable, he continued, There is a lack of appeal within the Montfleurois government to re-unite with Rosenmarkke, or vice versa,

Then we manufacture appeal! declared Meternisse, jumping from his seat.

And how. Do you. Expect. To do that? asked Mr. Z with a frown.

With the petition! declared Lambeau, slamming his cane into the ground as he stood, It is all circular Mr. Z! 

But a circle goes nowhere, retorted Z.

Only if it is not acted upon, replied Lambeau, And we are acting upon it! I propose a vote at next weeks meeting to form a commission to oversee the collection of grievances, he said, From there we will write out a proper ideological plan, 

What a chad, what a chad! clapped a gentleman from the corner of the room who was sitting beside one of the windows.

Very well then, if no one has rebuttal to this plan, I propose we do this, replied the president, looking around the room as the men in their seats muttered to each other, a few shaking their heads.

We shall take a vote on this? asked Meternisse.

Yes, yes, of course, replied the President, A vote!

The vote would barely pass the majority, with 34 Yea and 16 nays to the idea that Lambeau had proposed; however, this would be enough to set up the next meeting for the next week.

[b][i]Random lore tidbit[/i][/b]
Air New Westmore's larger airplanes, such as its Boeing 777s and Airbus A330s, are typically named after notable figures, founding values or locations within the country. Of note are the series of Boeing 777-200ERs named after members of the Dreemurr family, who are known for creating one of the oldest companies in the country, the Dreemurr Corporation. The planes bearing their names are NW-OAS (Asriel), NW-UDR (Chara), NW-DKR (Asgore) and NW-ZLJ (Toriel). NW-UDR was destroyed in a fatal crash in 2004 while serving as the ill-fated Flight 191, causing its sister aircraft to all be renamed to founding values such as "Friendship," "Determination," and "Brotherhood" for a period of time; their original names were later restored in late 2015. Another notable series of airplanes with ship names are the company's Boeing 777-300ER fleet, which all carry ship names starting with "Spirit of" - examples include NW-DAK (Spirit of Determination), NW-OKK (Spirit of Benevolence), NW-ASH (Spirit of Bravery), and the company's flagship airplane, NW-EST (Spirit of New Westmore).

Air New Westmore's custom of giving ship names to its airplanes is inherited from its early days as ACSW. Frederick Mansell, the founder of the airline, originally gave names to his aircraft as a way to adapt the longstanding naval tradition of naming vessels to the new technology. While all of its airplanes were named for most of the airline's operational history, starting from the 1990s only its widebody airplanes began to carry printed ship names.

[b]The Pirn government plans to merge administrative regions.
[sub]Le gouvernement de Pirn prévoit de fusionner des régions administratives.[/b][/sub]
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────[/list]

[i][b]P I R N ─[/b][/i] On 02 June, the [b]Pirn Parliament[/b] unveiled a proposal known as the [b]Merger Plan,[/b] or simply [b]Plan 8,[/b] aiming to consolidate the countrys administrative regions from 13 down to 8. The plan also includes consideration of granting [b]Victoria Region[/b] on [b]Chester Island [i](Bésart)[/i][/b] autonomous status under the name [b]Autonomous Region of Victoria[/b]. This is regarded as one of the most sweeping administrative reforms in Pirns history since the last major restructuring in 1963. Not only would the number of regions be reduced, but Pirn would, for the first time, establish a single autonomous region. According to policymakers, the current number of regions has become excessive and no longer reflects Pirns present circumstances. Meanwhile, the push to grant Victoria a degree of autonomy stems from its demographic makeup, where human residents significantly outnumber furry citizens.

Nevertheless, the plan has sparked considerable controversy. Many residents in several regions fear losing their local identities, and lawmakers caution that the merger must be approached with careful planning to avoid transferring old regional problems directly onto newly formed ones.

▌[i]I believe we must examine this merger seriously and cautiously. Such a move risks not only fueling public dissatisfaction but also placing an immediate burden on the new regional authorities if the issues of the old regions are suddenly passed on after consolidation. For example, Region Rupert currently suffers from severely underdeveloped infrastructure, yet it is slated to merge with the rapidly growing Orange Region. This merger would almost certainly slow Oranges momentum. Residents from Rupert would likely flock to Orange, causing population declines in several Rupert provinces while Orange struggles to cope with a sudden surge of migrants,[/i] independent MP [i]Simonette Lévêque[/i] said before Parliament.

For now, Plan 8 remains in the proposal stage and continues to undergo revisions, scrutiny, and debate within Parliament. Public opinion is sharply divided: supporters view it as a turning point that could reshape Pirns future, while critics warn that the risks are too great, concerns amplified by Lévêques remarks, particularly the fear that newly merged regions may be forced to shoulder the economic or social burdens of troubled former regions.

[list]──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[b]Prime Minister Jackson Rearden was removed from office in a parliamentary vote of confidence.
[sub]Le Premier ministre Jackson Rearden a été destitué par un vote de confiance du Parlement.[/b][/sub]
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────[/list]

On 27 May, a political earthquake shook Pirn as Prime Minister [i]Jackson Rearden[/i] was ousted in a confidence vote initiated by opposition factions in Parliament. Rearden was removed with 76% voting in favor [i](vote of no confidence)[/i] of his dismissal, while only 30% voted against [i](vote of confidence)[/i], and the remainder abstained. With this outcome, Rearden officially becomes the first prime minister in more than two decades to be forced out of office, the last being former Prime Minister [i]Lancelot Martel[/i] in 2000. According to political analysts, the fall of the Rearden government was unforeseen, prompting widespread surprise and speculation over possible ballot irregularities.

▌[i]I was shocked when I learned that Reardens government had been voted out. While Im aware that he made mistakes in certain policies, particularly in economics and social affairs, he did succeed in creating more job opportunities for recent graduates, curbing runaway oil prices, and addressing a number of environmental and corruption issues,[/i] said [i]Thalia Valdez[/i], Associate Professor of Political Science and Economics at the Pirn University of Politics and Economics, in an interview with reporters. Valdez expressed surprise and noted that Reardens downfall had been largely unexpected even among seasoned observers.

Meanwhile, social media and public discourse erupted. Reardens supporters voiced disappointment over his removal, while opposition supporters celebrated the outcome. Yet the prime ministers ouster has also heightened anxiety among many citizens, who fear signs of political instability. Although [i]Monica Franklin[/i] was swiftly appointed the new prime minister, becoming the first woman in Pirns history to hold the office, the move has done little to assuage public concern.
